帕倫達格竹笛主要由當地棉蘭老島的竹材製成，採用中空竹管作為主體結構。竹子經過風乾: The pulalu is mostly made from bamboo of local Mindanao, using a hollow bamboo tube as the main structure. Once air-dried, the bamboo has good acoustic properties. The body keeps the bamboo nodes, which form natural soundholes and resonating chambers. The mouth end uses the lip-valley flute design and must be ground precisely for efficient sound production. The surface may carry simple incised decoration, and on some versions the joints may be fixed with natural resin or plaited grass thread. It contains no metal fittings at all, relying entirely on the natural properties of the bamboo.
帕倫達格竹笛屬氣鳴樂器，霍恩博斯特尔–薩克斯編號 421.141.12，見於菲律: The pulalu is an aerophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 421.141.12, found in the Philippines. The lower end of the blowing end is cut at a slant to take the lower lip, and a second slant forms the blowing edge. To play, the lips must seal against the end of the flute so that the airstream glances across the edge. A beginner can first set the lower lip in the slant cut, then adjust the angle of lip valley and edge and steady the airstream; because it demands a precise embouchure, it is hard to make sound on.
帕倫達格竹笛起源於菲律賓南部的棉蘭老島地區，主要流行於摩洛人、馬諾博人、曼薩卡人: The pulalu originates in the Mindanao region of the southern Philippines and is mainly current among indigenous peoples such as the Moro, Manobo, Mansaka, Bagobo, Bukidnon and Banuwaen. The instrument is one of the most representative of Philippine bamboo flute culture and reflects the region's rich musical tradition. Its development is closely tied to the instrument-making craft of Mindanao, where makers drew on the abundant local bamboo and gradually refined their technique. As the largest bamboo flute used by the Moro, it holds an important place in tribal ritual, folk music and daily life. Its influence gradually spread to other parts of the Philippines, giving rise to several local variants and smaller sizes. Its intricate technique makes it the most challenging instrument of the old bamboo flute tradition, and it has been handed down from generation to generation to this day.

As the largest bamboo flute of the Moro it lies low, its tone weighty and penetrating with a natural bamboo warmth. Because of the lip-valley design its timbre is more sombre than the tumpong's and has more depth of resonance than the suling's. What sets it apart is that it takes precise control of lip tension to sound at all, which gives the tone a certain softness without losing the roughness characteristic of the region. The volume is moderate but it carries well, and outdoors it cuts through surrounding noise. Its overall timbre lies between the brightness of flutes and the warmth of reed instruments, and it has a distinctly Southeast Asian folk character.

The pulalu (also called palendag) is a bamboo aerophone of the Philippines, Hornbostel–Sachs 421.141.12. The lower end of its blowing end is cut at a slant to take the lower lip, and a second slant forms the blowing edge, making it a lip-valley flute; because it must be sounded with the lips sealed against the end, it is considered the hardest to use of the three bamboo flutes, with the tumpong and the suling. The Maguindanao use the largest of them, while the Bukidnon have the Hulakteb, of the same construction and about three-quarters the length. The Maguindanao play it at intimate family gatherings in the evening.
